\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy by 18+pp compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more diagnostic information.
\emph{Why does more information impair SFT learning?}

Prior work found no single trace representation consistently outperforms others \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, enabling controlled component ablation that directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning efficiency.
This proxy task aligns with prior *CL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction on LLM-generated Python code.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose trace representations into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\% across four models) underperform compact exception events (${\geq}$99.33\%) by 18+pp despite containing all diagnostic information, directly demonstrating that more information impairs SFT learning efficiency.
Training dynamics confirm the mechanism: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps, while \texttt{full\_trace} with label-only loss (gradient dilution reduced) oscillates (82--89\%) throughout training without reaching stable accuracy (Figure~\ref{fig:training_dynamics}).

A preliminary decomposition (Qwen family, 2 scales, 3 seeds each) provides an upper-bound estimate: gradient dilution accounts for at most ${\sim}$26\% of the gap, with the remainder reflecting information overload, though label-only loss simultaneously alters gradient selection, regularization, and training signal distribution (\S\ref{sec:density}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep across all four models reveals a sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$500 tokens, crossing the globals module dump threshold (${\sim}$384 tokens) and exposing structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values).
Even on silent logic errors (55.5\% of failures), exception events maintain 100\% recall because test assertions generate exception events.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces actively impair SFT learning}: training dynamics directly show the mechanism: verbose traces cause overfitting to spurious patterns, with \texttt{full\_trace} oscillating (82--89\%) without stable convergence even when gradient dilution is eliminated. Seed variance negatively correlates with input density ($\sigma{=}$0.00 for \texttt{exception\_only} to 4.48 for \texttt{no\_trace}), and SFT closes a 6--49pp zero-shot gap across all models (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
\item \textbf{Exception events are the minimal sufficient signal}: ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models and all seeds tested (1.5B--13B, three families), with ${\sim}$91\% semantic rather than format-driven (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}). Supplementary OOD analysis on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) preserves the ranking, though margins narrow due to ceiling effects (\S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Preliminary decomposition of the full-trace degradation}: a label-only loss ablation on the Qwen family (7B and 1.5B, 3 seeds each) provides an upper-bound estimate: gradient dilution ${\leq}$26\%, information overload ${\geq}$74\%, though the ablation simultaneously changes multiple training dynamics (\S\ref{sec:density}). A budget sweep across four models reveals a sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$500 tail tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy validated across four models and three architecture families}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) achieve ${\geq}$98.53\% across all four models with non-overlapping CIs against Tier~2; Tier~2 (loop compression, 77--86\%) is model-dependent: Qwen +10.9/+7.2pp (7B/1.5B), DeepSeek +7.0pp, CodeLlama +0.9pp (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate across two research questions:
4	(1)~Why do complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy despite containing all diagnostic information?
5	(2)~Which trace components carry the verdict signal, and how does their density affect learning?
6	All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Problem-level partition (472 train / 119 test, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). \texttt{exception\_only} duplicates (48.99\% test; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}) arise from within-problem variants; deduplication yields 0.00pp delta. Problem-level clustered bootstrap CIs are ${\sim}2\times$ wider but all Tier~1 vs.\ Tier~2 gaps (${\geq}$12pp) remain significant ($p{<}.001$).}
7	Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}.0001$ unless noted.
8

45	\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}
46	Under \texttt{exception\_only}, all four models achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all seeds: Qwen-7B (99.83\%$\pm$0.00, 3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B (99.83\%), CodeLlama-13B (99.89\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; seed 123 achieves 100\%), and DeepSeek-6.7B (99.39\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds).
47	The cross-model range is 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), the tightest of any condition.

49	\paragraph{Exception signals across model scales.}
50	Tier~1 signals are scale-invariant across 1.5B--13B (8.7$\times$): \texttt{exception\_only} spans 0.50pp (99.33--99.89\%) and \texttt{ae\_only} 1.18pp (98.74--99.92\%).
51	CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\%, confirming the 2 persistent errors (\texttt{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}) are convergence artifacts; 99.83\% is a floor, not a ceiling.
52	Scale effects concentrate in Tier~2: \texttt{loop\_only} spans 8.57pp (77.06--85.63\%), with CodeLlama-13B below Qwen-1.5B, suggesting architecture matters more than parameter count for lower-density signals.
53	In contrast, \texttt{no\_trace} scales with capacity (72.35--76.47\%, Figure~\ref{fig:cross_scale}) and shows the highest seed variance ($\sigma{=}$4.48pp).

62	\paragraph{VOTA cross-family variation.}
63	Excluding outlier seeds, VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all four models (0.80pp range).
64	DeepSeek seed 42 (84.45\%) is a tokenizer-driven truncation failure (91.7\% of samples exceed 2{,}048 tokens after tokenization; Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}), demonstrating that VOTA's longer sequences are sensitive to tokenizer efficiency: 1/4 models suffers catastrophic truncation under standard training length. \texttt{exception\_only}'s compact inputs (median 150 tokens) sidestep this vulnerability entirely.

66	\subsection{Component Ablation}
67	\label{sec:ablation}
68	
69	Multi-seed \texttt{ae\_only} ablations use Qwen-7B; \texttt{loop\_only} is evaluated across three models to test Tier~2 generalization (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
70	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} decomposes VOTA on Qwen-2.5-7B and reveals a two-tier hierarchy validated across all four models and three architecture families (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}): Tier~1 (${\geq}$98.53\%) and Tier~2 (77--86\%) are separated by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs.

Entries marked $^\dag$/$^\S$/$^\ddag$ are 3-seed mean$\pm$std; unmarked entries are single seed (seed 42). Per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}. Seed $\sigma$ negatively correlates with density (0.00 for exception to 0.52 for loop).}

98	Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%$\pm$0.00) exceeds VOTA (99.05\%$\pm$0.38) by +0.78pp (2/3 seeds $p{<}.05$, all directionally consistent), implying that combining signals introduces noise.
99	Removing assertion points has no effect (\texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae} = 99.41\%, single seed), confirming exception dominance.
100	The Tier~1/2 boundary is unambiguous: the lowest Tier~1 condition (\texttt{ae\_only} on DeepSeek, 98.53\%$\pm$0.30, 2 seeds) exceeds the highest Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only} on Qwen-7B, 86.05\%, CI [83.97, 87.96]) by 12.48\,pp with non-overlapping confidence intervals.
101	Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} lifts over \texttt{no\_trace} are model-dependent: Qwen shows +10.92pp (7B) and +7.19pp (1.5B, $p{<}.0001$), with the larger 7B gain likely reflecting greater capacity to exploit structured loop patterns; DeepSeek +6.95pp (80.31\%), CodeLlama +0.93pp (77.40\%, n.s.).
102	\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}
103	The strongest non-trivial regex heuristic (B4: exception class name matching; Table~\ref{tab:regex}) achieves 93.61\% accuracy (F1=0.876), trailing SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%, F1=0.997) by 6.22pp (McNemar $p{<}.001$).
104	The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
105	Across all formats, SFT outperforms the best applicable regex by +3.62--23.86pp (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
106	
107	\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
108	Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range); three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp.
109	SFT compresses this range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
110	\paragraph{Frontier model crossover.}
111	Two frontier models confirm that SFT's advantage depends on input density.
112	GPT-4o zero-shot achieves 87.98\% on \texttt{exception\_only} and 84.45\% on \texttt{no\_trace}; GPT-4.1 achieves 82.18\% and 77.31\%, respectively.
113	Under \texttt{no\_trace}, both frontier models outperform SFT Qwen-7B (75.13\%) by +9.32pp (GPT-4o) and +2.18pp (GPT-4.1).
114	Under \texttt{exception\_only}, the ranking reverses: SFT Qwen-7B (99.83\%) exceeds GPT-4o by 11.85pp and GPT-4.1 by 17.65pp.
115	This crossover shows that compact diagnostic input unlocks SFT's full advantage, while absent or verbose traces favor general reasoning capacity.
116	
117	\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
118	\label{sec:nomarker}
119	
120	The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
121	To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).
122	
123	Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
124	Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
125	The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
126	Regex baselines confirm this decomposition: B5 (\texttt{[No exception data]}$\to$pass, 99.33\% with markers) collapses to 28.49\% without markers, confirming it is entirely format-dependent.
127	The strongest semantic regex B4 (exception class matching, 93.61\%) is marker-invariant; SFT \texttt{nomarker} (97.65\%) exceeds it by 4.04pp, isolating the learned semantic contribution beyond pattern matching.
128	
129	\subsection{Preliminary Decomposition of the Full-Trace Gap}
130	\label{sec:density}
131	
132	The 17.61pp gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.44\%$\pm$1.08, 3-seed mean) and VOTA (99.05\%, 3-seed mean) can be probed via \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} (85.94\%$\pm$1.12, 3 seeds; Table~\ref{tab:density}), which retains the full trace but masks all trace tokens from the loss.
133	
134	\begin{table}[t]
135	\centering
136	\caption{Preliminary decomposition of the full-trace gap (Qwen-7B, 3-seed means). Label-only loss provides an upper-bound estimate of gradient dilution (${\leq}$26\%); the ablation simultaneously changes gradient selection, regularization, and signal distribution.}
137	\label{tab:density}
138	\small
139	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
140	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
141	\toprule
142	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
143	\midrule
144	full\_trace & 81.44{\scriptsize$\pm$1.08} & --- & --- \\
145	label\_only & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.50pp & 26\% \\
146	VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & +17.61pp & 100\% \\
147	\bottomrule
148	\end{tabular}%
149	}
150	\end{table}
151	
152	Label-only loss improves accuracy by +4.50pp (3-seed mean), providing an upper-bound estimate that gradient dilution accounts for at most ${\sim}$26\% of the gap.
153	However, this ablation simultaneously changes which tokens receive gradients, removes implicit regularization from trace prediction, and alters the training signal distribution; the +4.50pp may partially reflect these confounds rather than gradient dilution alone.
154	The remaining ${\sim}$74\% (+13.11pp) reflects information overload at inference: the model receives thousands of irrelevant trace lines that compete for attention with the diagnostic signal, regardless of loss design.
155	Cross-model evidence supports this: the tail-truncation sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}, all four models) crosses the globals module dump threshold, exposing structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values).
156	Cross-scale validation on Qwen-1.5B yields a consistent pattern (17\% gradient dilution, 83\% information overload, 3 seeds), confirming that information overload dominates across model scales.
157	CodeLlama-13B and DeepSeek-6.7B both exhibit label-only collapse (28.5\% accuracy, collapsing to the minority class), limiting the decomposition to models whose tokenizers preserve sufficient trace structure under the training sequence length.
158	Error analysis provides direct evidence: all 217 \texttt{full\_trace} errors occur in samples where tokenizer truncation removes diagnostic markers, and among the 61 samples where \texttt{full\_trace} underperforms \texttt{no\_trace}, all exhibit the same truncation pattern, confirming that information overload manifests through a mechanical truncation pathway rather than semantic confusion.
159	The 26\%/74\% attribution is a preliminary upper-bound estimate limited to the Qwen family (2 scales, 3 seeds each); the two factors may interact, and label-only loss changes multiple optimization dynamics simultaneously.
160	
161	\subsection{Additional Analyses}
162	\label{sec:additional}
163	
164	\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
165	\label{sec:trace_length}
166	Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
167	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).
168	
169	\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
170	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).
171	All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp), indicating that signal-poor conditions produce a shared performance floor regardless of scale or architecture.
172	
173	A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a sharp performance jump localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
174	At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--80.7\%, only +1.0--4.8pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+13.2--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
175	This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, crossing the globals module dump threshold (${\sim}$384 tokens) and exposing structured execution markers (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
176	CodeLlama tail conditions use label-only loss (\S\ref{sec:density}); cross-model tail comparisons should account for this training difference.
177	Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations confirms all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
178	\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
179	The residual 2--5pp gap confirms that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).
180	
181	\paragraph{Calibration.}

\section{Experiments}

We evaluate across two research questions:
(1)~Why do complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy despite containing all diagnostic information?
(2)~Which trace components carry the verdict signal, and how does their density affect learning?
All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% CIs.\footnote{Problem-level partition (472 train / 119 test, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). \texttt{exception\_only} duplicates (48.99\% test; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}) arise from within-problem variants; deduplication yields 0.00pp delta. Problem-level clustered bootstrap CIs are ${\sim}2\times$ wider but all Tier~1 vs.\ Tier~2 gaps (${\geq}$12pp) remain significant ($p{<}.001$).}
Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}.0001$ unless noted.

\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

Table~\ref{tab:cross_model} compares four models spanning an 8.7$\times$ parameter range (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families (Qwen, DeepSeek, CodeLlama) under key conditions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Cross-model verdict accuracy (\%, $N{=}1{,}190$) across four models (1.5B--13B) and three architecture families. Multi-seed entries report mean$\pm$std over 2--3 seeds; $^\dag$ = single seed (seed 42). Bold: best per model. Full per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}; per-class metrics in Appendix~\ref{sec:per_class}.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Qwen-7B} & \textbf{Qwen-1.5B} & \textbf{CL-13B} & \textbf{DS-6.7B} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.83}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & \textbf{99.89}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} & \textbf{99.39}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.10} \\
ae\_only & 99.64{\scriptsize$\pm$0.49} & 98.83{\scriptsize$\pm$0.36} & 99.08{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & 98.53{\scriptsize$\pm$0.30} \\
VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & 99.54{\scriptsize$\pm$0.06} & 98.74{\scriptsize$\pm$0.24} & 99.25$^\ddag$ \\
loop\_only & 86.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.52} & 79.54{\scriptsize$\pm$1.42} & 77.40{\scriptsize$\pm$1.54} & 80.31{\scriptsize$\pm$1.65} \\
full\_trace & 81.44{\scriptsize$\pm$1.11} & 77.06$^\dag$ & 79.9$^\S$ & 79.16$^\dag$ \\
no\_trace & 75.13$^\dag$ & 72.35{\scriptsize$\pm$4.48} & 76.47$^\dag$ & 73.36$^\dag$ \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & \multicolumn{4}{c}{71.51} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\vspace{2pt}
\par\raggedright\footnotesize
DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} 3 seeds: 99.33/99.50/99.33 ($\sigma{=}$0.10pp).
VOTA on Qwen-7B: 99.41/98.66/99.08 ($\sigma{=}$0.38).
\texttt{ae\_only} 3 seeds: 99.92/99.08/99.92 (mean 99.64\%); Qwen-7B \texttt{loop\_only} 3 seeds: 85.63/85.88/86.64 (mean 86.05\%).
Qwen-1.5B \texttt{exception\_only}: 99.83\% across 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}$0).
$^\ddag$DeepSeek VOTA 3 seeds: 84.45/99.16/99.33; seed 42 (84.45\%, fail recall\,=\,45.4\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-driven truncation (Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}), reported as 2-seed mean.
$^\S$CodeLlama \texttt{full\_trace} not available; head-2048 proxy (79.9\%) reported.
\end{table}

\paragraph{Exception dominance across families.}
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, all four models achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all seeds: Qwen-7B (99.83\%$\pm$0.00, 3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B (99.83\%), CodeLlama-13B (99.89\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; seed 123 achieves 100\%), and DeepSeek-6.7B (99.39\%$\pm$0.10, 3 seeds).
The cross-model range is 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), the tightest of any condition.

\paragraph{Exception signals across model scales.}
Tier~1 signals are scale-invariant across 1.5B--13B (8.7$\times$): \texttt{exception\_only} spans 0.50pp (99.33--99.89\%) and \texttt{ae\_only} 1.18pp (98.74--99.92\%).
CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\%, confirming the 2 persistent errors (\texttt{GeneratorExit}; Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}) are convergence artifacts; 99.83\% is a floor, not a ceiling.
Scale effects concentrate in Tier~2: \texttt{loop\_only} spans 8.57pp (77.06--85.63\%), with CodeLlama-13B below Qwen-1.5B, suggesting architecture matters more than parameter count for lower-density signals.
In contrast, \texttt{no\_trace} scales with capacity (72.35--76.47\%, Figure~\ref{fig:cross_scale}) and shows the highest seed variance ($\sigma{=}$4.48pp).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_cross_model_gap}
\caption{Verdict accuracy vs.\ model scale. \texttt{exception\_only} maintains ${\geq}$99.33\% regardless of scale, while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic sensitivity (+4.12pp). \texttt{nomarker} (markers removed) shows no scale degradation.}
\label{fig:cross_scale}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{VOTA cross-family variation.}
Excluding outlier seeds, VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all four models (0.80pp range).
DeepSeek seed 42 (84.45\%) is a tokenizer-driven truncation failure (91.7\% of samples exceed 2{,}048 tokens after tokenization; Appendix~\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}), demonstrating that VOTA's longer sequences are sensitive to tokenizer efficiency: 1/4 models suffers catastrophic truncation under standard training length. \texttt{exception\_only}'s compact inputs (median 150 tokens) sidestep this vulnerability entirely.

\subsection{Component Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}

Multi-seed \texttt{ae\_only} ablations use Qwen-7B; \texttt{loop\_only} is evaluated across three models to test Tier~2 generalization (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} decomposes VOTA on Qwen-2.5-7B and reveals a two-tier hierarchy validated across all four models and three architecture families (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}): Tier~1 (${\geq}$98.53\%) and Tier~2 (77--86\%) are separated by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Component ablation on Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$). Tier~1 signals achieve near-perfect accuracy; combining them (VOTA) slightly dilutes performance. Entries marked $^\dag$/$^\S$/$^\ddag$ are 3-seed mean$\pm$std; unmarked entries are single seed (seed 42). Per-seed breakdowns in Appendix~\ref{sec:full_results}. Seed $\sigma$ negatively correlates with density (0.00 for exception to 0.52 for loop).}
\label{tab:ablation}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{llccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Components} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Tier} \\
\midrule
ae\_only & assertion-point & 99.64$^\dag$ & [99.26, 99.87] & 1 \\
exception\_only & exception events & \textbf{99.83} & [99.58, 100.00] & 1 \\
VOTA & exc+ae+loop & 99.05$^\S$ & [98.49, 99.50] & --- \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & exc+loop & 99.41 & [98.90, 99.80] & --- \\
loop\_only & loop compression & 86.05$^\ddag$ & [83.97, 87.96] & 2 \\
full\_trace & complete trace & 81.44{\scriptsize$\pm$1.08} & --- & --- \\
no\_trace & none & 75.13 & [72.77, 77.48] & --- \\
\midrule
Regex (best) & exc.\ type regex & 93.61 & --- & --- \\
3-shot (Qwen-7B) & in-context learning & 90.84 & --- & --- \\
Zero-shot (4 models) & prompting & 51.0--93.5 & --- & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%$\pm$0.00) exceeds VOTA (99.05\%$\pm$0.38) by +0.78pp (2/3 seeds $p{<}.05$, all directionally consistent), implying that combining signals introduces noise.
Removing assertion points has no effect (\texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae} = 99.41\%, single seed), confirming exception dominance.
The Tier~1/2 boundary is unambiguous: the lowest Tier~1 condition (\texttt{ae\_only} on DeepSeek, 98.53\%$\pm$0.30, 2 seeds) exceeds the highest Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only} on Qwen-7B, 86.05\%, CI [83.97, 87.96]) by 12.48\,pp with non-overlapping confidence intervals.
Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} lifts over \texttt{no\_trace} are model-dependent: Qwen shows +10.92pp (7B) and +7.19pp (1.5B, $p{<}.0001$), with the larger 7B gain likely reflecting greater capacity to exploit structured loop patterns; DeepSeek +6.95pp (80.31\%), CodeLlama +0.93pp (77.40\%, n.s.).
\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}
The strongest non-trivial regex heuristic (B4: exception class name matching; Table~\ref{tab:regex}) achieves 93.61\% accuracy (F1=0.876), trailing SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%, F1=0.997) by 6.22pp (McNemar $p{<}.001$).
The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
Across all formats, SFT outperforms the best applicable regex by +3.62--23.86pp (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range); three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp.
SFT compresses this range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
\paragraph{Frontier model crossover.}
Two frontier models confirm that SFT's advantage depends on input density.
GPT-4o zero-shot achieves 87.98\% on \texttt{exception\_only} and 84.45\% on \texttt{no\_trace}; GPT-4.1 achieves 82.18\% and 77.31\%, respectively.
Under \texttt{no\_trace}, both frontier models outperform SFT Qwen-7B (75.13\%) by +9.32pp (GPT-4o) and +2.18pp (GPT-4.1).
Under \texttt{exception\_only}, the ranking reverses: SFT Qwen-7B (99.83\%) exceeds GPT-4o by 11.85pp and GPT-4.1 by 17.65pp.
This crossover shows that compact diagnostic input unlocks SFT's full advantage, while absent or verbose traces favor general reasoning capacity.

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
Regex baselines confirm this decomposition: B5 (\texttt{[No exception data]}$\to$pass, 99.33\% with markers) collapses to 28.49\% without markers, confirming it is entirely format-dependent.
The strongest semantic regex B4 (exception class matching, 93.61\%) is marker-invariant; SFT \texttt{nomarker} (97.65\%) exceeds it by 4.04pp, isolating the learned semantic contribution beyond pattern matching.

\subsection{Preliminary Decomposition of the Full-Trace Gap}
\label{sec:density}

The 17.61pp gap between \texttt{full\_trace} (81.44\%$\pm$1.08, 3-seed mean) and VOTA (99.05\%, 3-seed mean) can be probed via \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only} (85.94\%$\pm$1.12, 3 seeds; Table~\ref{tab:density}), which retains the full trace but masks all trace tokens from the loss.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Preliminary decomposition of the full-trace gap (Qwen-7B, 3-seed means). Label-only loss provides an upper-bound estimate of gradient dilution (${\leq}$26\%); the ablation simultaneously changes gradient selection, regularization, and signal distribution.}
\label{tab:density}
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$ vs.\ full\_trace} & \textbf{Gap explained} \\
\midrule
full\_trace & 81.44{\scriptsize$\pm$1.08} & --- & --- \\
label\_only & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.50pp & 26\% \\
VOTA & 99.05{\scriptsize$\pm$0.38} & +17.61pp & 100\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Label-only loss improves accuracy by +4.50pp (3-seed mean), providing an upper-bound estimate that gradient dilution accounts for at most ${\sim}$26\% of the gap.
However, this ablation simultaneously changes which tokens receive gradients, removes implicit regularization from trace prediction, and alters the training signal distribution; the +4.50pp may partially reflect these confounds rather than gradient dilution alone.
The remaining ${\sim}$74\% (+13.11pp) reflects information overload at inference: the model receives thousands of irrelevant trace lines that compete for attention with the diagnostic signal, regardless of loss design.
Cross-model evidence supports this: the tail-truncation sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$500 tokens (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}, all four models) crosses the globals module dump threshold, exposing structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values).
Cross-scale validation on Qwen-1.5B yields a consistent pattern (17\% gradient dilution, 83\% information overload, 3 seeds), confirming that information overload dominates across model scales.
CodeLlama-13B and DeepSeek-6.7B both exhibit label-only collapse (28.5\% accuracy, collapsing to the minority class), limiting the decomposition to models whose tokenizers preserve sufficient trace structure under the training sequence length.
Error analysis provides direct evidence: all 217 \texttt{full\_trace} errors occur in samples where tokenizer truncation removes diagnostic markers, and among the 61 samples where \texttt{full\_trace} underperforms \texttt{no\_trace}, all exhibit the same truncation pattern, confirming that information overload manifests through a mechanical truncation pathway rather than semantic confusion.
The 26\%/74\% attribution is a preliminary upper-bound estimate limited to the Qwen family (2 scales, 3 seeds each); the two factors may interact, and label-only loss changes multiple optimization dynamics simultaneously.

\subsection{Additional Analyses}
\label{sec:additional}

\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
\label{sec:trace_length}
Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).

\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).
All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp), indicating that signal-poor conditions produce a shared performance floor regardless of scale or architecture.

A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a sharp performance jump localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--80.7\%, only +1.0--4.8pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+13.2--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, crossing the globals module dump threshold (${\sim}$384 tokens) and exposing structured execution markers (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
CodeLlama tail conditions use label-only loss (\S\ref{sec:density}); cross-model tail comparisons should account for this training difference.
Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations confirms all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
The residual 2--5pp gap confirms that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).

\paragraph{Calibration.}
\label{sec:calibration}
Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
This calibration advantage generalizes across architectures and scales: all four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.005 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Table~\ref{tab:calibration_model_level} in Appendix), indicating well-calibrated predictions rather than overfit confidence.

\paragraph{Error analysis.}
\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}); per-type breakdown confirms all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy, with only \texttt{GeneratorExit} (a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass) causing failures (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}).

\paragraph{Length control.}
Padding \texttt{exception\_only} to 2{,}048 tokens, even in a semantically loaded position (after the verdict region), yields identical accuracy (99.83\%), confirming the 18+pp gap arises from spurious patterns in verbose trace content, not sequence length.

\paragraph{Supplementary OOD analysis.}
\label{sec:debugbench}
On DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench} ($N{=}426$), the condition ranking is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} 100\%, VOTA 99.77\%, \texttt{no\_trace} 96.71\%.
However, narrow margins (3.29pp headroom from \texttt{no\_trace}) limit discriminative power; this supplementary analysis confirms the ranking but cannot establish effect sizes comparable to the primary dataset (Appendix~\ref{sec:debugbench_full}).

1	\section{Method}
2	
3	\subsection{Task Definition and Diagnostic Signal Metrics}
4	
5	We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.
6	The model produces a single token (\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}), making this a binary classification task.
7	Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution, providing cleaner ablation contrasts than generation tasks.
8	
9	To quantify signal quality without circular reference to model accuracy, we define the \emph{diagnostic token ratio} $d = n_{\text{diag}} / n_{\text{total}}$, where $n_{\text{diag}}$ counts tokens matching exception or assertion patterns.
10	This model-free metric correlates with accuracy at Pearson $r{=}0.949$ ($p{=}0.014$, $N{=}5$ main conditions), but captures only the \emph{explicit} diagnostic pathway; tail-truncated conditions achieve 93--97\% with $d {\approx} 0$, indicating a second, implicit signal channel operating through terminal execution state (\S\ref{sec:density}).
11	
12	\subsection{Dataset}
13	\label{sec:dataset}
14	
15	We sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \texttt{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\% pass, 33\% fail).
16	The dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\%).
17	The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\% train, 48.99\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).
18	
19	\subsection{Trace Representations}
20	
21	We define seven conditions that vary the trace information available (Figure~\ref{fig:trace_overview}):
22	\begin{itemize}
23	\item \texttt{no\_trace}: Source code and test input only.
24	\item \texttt{full\_trace}: Complete line-by-line trace with variable states.
25	\item \texttt{VOTA} (Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction): Exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).
26	\item \texttt{exception\_only}: Only exception/error events.
27	\item \texttt{ae\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected pairs.
28	\item \texttt{loop\_only}: Only loop compression summaries.
29	\item \texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.
30	\end{itemize}
31	
32	\begin{figure*}[t]
33	\centering
34	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}
35	\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace. Four conditions vary the trace information: \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%), \texttt{full\_trace} (81.44\%), VOTA (99.05\%), and \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%). Accuracies for Qwen-2.5-7B ($N{=}1{,}190$); multi-seed means where available (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}). Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_examples} provides input/output examples.}
36	\label{fig:trace_overview}
37	\end{figure*}
38	
39	\subsection{Models and Training}
40	
41	We evaluate four models spanning three architecture families: \textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct} \citep{qwen2024coder}, \textbf{CodeLlama-13B-Instruct} \citep{roziere2024code}, and \textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \citep{deepseek2024coder}, covering a 1.5B--13B parameter range (8.7$\times$).
42	All conditions use LoRA \citep{hu2022lora} (rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05) on all linear layers, 3 epochs, effective batch size 32, LR $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup/decay, max sequence length 2{,}048 tokens.
43	Sequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.
44	The primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \texttt{exception\_only} robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_details}).
45	
46	\subsection{Loss Ablation}
47	
48	To probe the contribution of gradient dilution, we introduce \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).
49	TRL's SFTTrainer computes mean cross-entropy over label tokens, so label-only loss does not amplify the effective learning rate.
50	However, this ablation simultaneously changes three variables: (1)~which tokens receive gradient updates, (2)~the implicit regularization from predicting trace tokens, and (3)~the training signal distribution.
51	The resulting improvement over standard \texttt{full\_trace} provides an \emph{upper-bound estimate} of gradient dilution's contribution; the remaining gap to VOTA reflects information overload at inference, but the decomposition is approximate (\S\ref{sec:density}).

1	\section{Introduction}
2	
3	Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
4	The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
5	Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
6	Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.
7	
8	Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
9	Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
10	This approach aligns with recent *CL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.
11	
12	We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
13	Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.
14	
15	The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone (${\sim}$73--76\%) while exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models and seeds (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
16	A simple regex baseline (B5) that exploits the \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} format marker matches this ceiling at 99.33\%; even a trivial pattern suffices, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
17	Marker removal collapses B5 to 28.49\% while SFT retains 97.65\% ($-$2.01pp); cross-dataset transfer at 99.41\% (HumanEval${\to}$MBPP) confirms that SFT acquires genuine diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).
18	
19	A preliminary decomposition on the Qwen family (7B and 1.5B, 3 seeds each) provides a confounded upper-bound estimate: gradient dilution accounts for ${\leq}$26\% of the gap, with diagnostic signal dilution (the mechanism underlying what is intuitively termed ``information overload'') at ${\geq}$74\%, though the label-only ablation simultaneously alters gradient selection, regularization, and effective learning rate (\S\ref{sec:density}).
20	Training dynamics confirm this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps, while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates between 82--89\% without stable convergence (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
21	A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$512 tokens; this threshold coincides with the globals module dump (${\sim}$384 tokens), beyond which structured \texttt{[Line~X]} variable values appear (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).
22	
23	Our contributions:
24	\begin{enumerate}
25	\item \textbf{Complete traces are strictly dominated by compact exception events}: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone (${\sim}$73--76\%) while exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}). Training dynamics directly show the mechanism: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without stable convergence (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
26	
27	\item \textbf{SFT learns genuine diagnostic patterns beyond format matching}: a regex exploiting format markers matches the exception ceiling (99.33\%), but marker removal collapses it to 28.49\% while SFT retains 97.65\% ($-$2.01pp); cross-dataset transfer at 99.41\% confirms the learned signal generalizes (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).
28

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *CL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone (${\sim}$73--76\%) while exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all models and seeds (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex baseline (B5) that exploits the \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} format marker matches this ceiling at 99.33\%; even a trivial pattern suffices, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses B5 to 28.49\% while SFT retains 97.65\% ($-$2.01pp); cross-dataset transfer at 99.41\% (HumanEval${\to}$MBPP) confirms that SFT acquires genuine diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

A preliminary decomposition on the Qwen family (7B and 1.5B, 3 seeds each) provides a confounded upper-bound estimate: gradient dilution accounts for ${\leq}$26\% of the gap, with diagnostic signal dilution (the mechanism underlying what is intuitively termed ``information overload'') at ${\geq}$74\%, though the label-only ablation simultaneously alters gradient selection, regularization, and effective learning rate (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics confirm this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps, while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates between 82--89\% without stable convergence (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance jump at ${\sim}$512 tokens; this threshold coincides with the globals module dump (${\sim}$384 tokens), beyond which structured \texttt{[Line~X]} variable values appear (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces are strictly dominated by compact exception events}: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone (${\sim}$73--76\%) while exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}). Training dynamics directly show the mechanism: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without stable convergence (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).

\item \textbf{SFT learns genuine diagnostic patterns beyond format matching}: a regex exploiting format markers matches the exception ceiling (99.33\%), but marker removal collapses it to 28.49\% while SFT retains 97.65\% ($-$2.01pp); cross-dataset transfer at 99.41\% confirms the learned signal generalizes (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

\item \textbf{A two-tier signal hierarchy with a practical trace selection strategy}: Tier~1 (exceptions, assertions; ${\geq}$98.53\%) dominates Tier~2 (loop compression; 77--86\%) by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs across all four models. A sharp performance transition at ${\sim}$512 tail tokens yields a practical fallback: exception events first, tail-truncated state otherwise (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

\item \textbf{Preliminary decomposition of the full-trace degradation}: a confounded upper-bound estimate via label-only loss on the Qwen family (7B and 1.5B, 3 seeds each) attributes gradient dilution ${\leq}$26\% and diagnostic signal dilution ${\geq}$74\% of the gap, though the ablation simultaneously alters gradient selection, regularization, and effective learning rate (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\end{enumerate}
